Paragraph:
Translation: O my teacher, behold the great army of the sons of Pandu, so expertly arranged by your intelligent disciple, the son of Drupada.

Purport (Excerpt): Duryodhana, a great diplomat, wanted to point out the defects of Dronacarya, the great brahmana commander-in-chief. ... Now, on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra, Dhrstadyumna took the side of the Pandavas, and it was he who arranged for their military phalanx, after having learned the art from Dronacarya. Duryodhana pointed out this mistake of Dronacarya's so that he might be alert and uncompromising in the fighting. By this he wanted to point out also that he should not be similarly lenient in battle against the Pandavas, who were also Dronacarya's affectionate students. ... Duryodhana also warned that such leniency in the fight would lead to defeat.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Duryodhana continues to feel deeply insecure about the strength of the Pandava army. He fears that his commander-in-chief, Dronacarya, might show leniency in battle because the opposing side consists of his beloved former students (especially Arjuna).
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Duryodhana resorts to political and psychological manipulation. He deliberately reminds Dronacarya that the enemy's military formation was arranged by Dhrstadyumna—a student Dronacarya magnanimously taught, despite knowing Dhrstadyumna was prophesied to kill him. Duryodhana uses this to provoke Dronacarya into fighting ruthlessly.
Outcome/Resolution: Through this calculated statement, Duryodhana attempts to eliminate any affection Dronacarya holds for the enemy, aiming to instill a sense of urgency and uncompromising aggression in his commander.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.relationship Challenges (Work): Power dynamics, Trust issues, Exploitation of loyalties

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Kutilata (Crookedness or deceitful diplomacy driven by selfish motives)
Bheda (The political strategy of creating division or exploiting rifts to maintain control)
Moha (Attachment, which Duryodhana fears Dronacarya will exhibit toward the Pandavas)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The verse highlights the contrast between Duryodhana's transactional, materially-driven consciousness and Dronacarya's earlier brahminical magnanimity. Duryodhana lacks understanding of pure duty (dharma), relying instead on diplomatic fault-finding and instigating worldly fears to motivate his commander.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Duryodhana exhibits Machiavellian personality traits, using psychological manipulation to manage his own severe anxiety. By intentionally triggering Dronacarya's past traumas and reminding him of a direct mortal threat (Dhrstadyumna), Duryodhana attempts to override Dronacarya's affection for the Pandavas with a survival instinct, ensuring brutal compliance on the battlefield.
